prize_parts.citation: for the invention and first experimental realisation of circuit quantum electrodynamics, bringing strong light-matter coupling to superconducting electrical circuits

statement.case_for: Circuit QED is a single, sharply defined idea with a before and after: place an artificial atom in an on-chip resonator, reach the strong-coupling regime, and read out and control the qubit dispersively. The 2004 theory and the 2004 strong-coupling experiment are two halves of one achievement, and the architecture is now the basis of essentially every superconducting processor, of quantum-limited amplification chains and of much of microwave quantum optics. Two decades of independent replication across laboratories and materials make the interpretation stable. The theory-plus-experiment structure maps naturally onto Girvin for the framework and Schoelkopf and Wallraff for the experimental realisation. Having read the colleagues' arguments, I keep this as my first choice, but I hold it with less confidence than the opening ranking implied because the case for B043 on maturity and cleanliness of attribution is strong.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is proximity to the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits; several colleagues will reasonably say the committee should not return to the same platform so soon. Attribution is also genuinely hard: the proposal was by five people, and any three-name cut leaves out Blais, whose claim is strong, and the credit within the Yale and ETH groups is intertwined. Finally, part of the impact is engineering of qubits rather than discovery of new physics.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks circuit QED fourth but warns that the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits makes a further award in the same area problematic, and that omitting Girvin from a three-person cut is a real cost.
responses.response: I take the timing point seriously and cannot dismiss it, since I am conflicted by proximity to the field. But the 2025 citation concerned macroscopic quantum tunnelling and energy quantisation in a Josephson circuit, a question about quantum mechanics at the macroscopic scale. Circuit QED is a different achievement, about light-matter coupling, readout and control, and it does not follow logically from or duplicate that prize. I agree on Girvin: I propose him with Schoelkopf and Wallraff, accepting that Blais is left out, and I regard this as the weakest part of the case and not something to wave away.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first because they transformed what can be measured and how accurately, with fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, a clean Katori and Ye attribution and good timing given the discussion on redefining the second.
responses.response: I agree with Kroll that B043 has the cleanest attribution and the strongest maturity case of anything on the list, and that is why I name it as my first alternative. Where I disagree is on discovery weight: a lattice clock is an extraordinary refinement of precision metrology, which the 2005 and 2012 prizes already honoured in neighbouring forms, whereas circuit QED opened a new regime of light-matter physics. I would not object to B043 being the consensus outcome if the attribution problems of B023 turn out to be unresolvable.

responses.point: Pearce puts IceCube neutrino astronomy first, as the opening of a new observational window, and ranks circuit QED only seventh.
responses.response: I accept that the diffuse flux is a real discovery and a major experimental feat, but the credit is spread over a very large collaboration and over AMANDA and other pioneers, and the source associations rest on evidence of only 3 to 4 sigma. That makes the three-name attribution less secure than for circuit QED, where the two defining 2004 papers are identifiable. I would ask Pearce what he sees as the decisive individual contribution to the discovery, and I would not rank B010 above B023 until that question has a firm answer.

responses.point: Olsson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first as a predicted flat-band condition followed by a decisive experiment, forming a natural theory-plus-experiment pairing.
responses.response: The theory-plus-experiment structure is attractive and I rank B029 sixth myself, so I do not dismiss it. My reservation is maturity: the pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is still unsettled and the field is under a decade old, while circuit QED has had two decades of confirmation and a stable interpretation. I would support B029 later, once the mechanism is better understood, but I think it is premature for this year.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a second superconducting-circuit prize within two years of the 2025 award.
How to cut four credited circuit QED names to three, and whether Blais should replace Girvin.
Whether B043 deserves to rank above B023 once discovery weight and attribution cleanliness are weighed together.
statement.conflict_note: Possible recusal issue: I direct WACQT and work at Chalmers in superconducting circuits and circuit and waveguide QED, and Chalmers colleagues such as Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson work in the same field and Chalmers hosted the 2025 laureates, so I have a professional connection to the community around B023 and should be treated as potentially conflicted on that candidate. No specific personal tie to the named B023 candidates is recorded in my profile.
